extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the Alice/Mayo two-part test (Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B), including the particular 'treatment or prophylaxis' consideration and the search for an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular treatment and prophylaxis consideration (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting a judicial exception is not directed to the judicial exception if it also recites additional element(s) demonstrating that the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application by applying or using the recited judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such application or use meaningfully limits the claim beyond merely linking the exception to a technological environment; these claims are eligible at Step 2A because they are not 'directed to' the exception. Examples include administration steps that use a natural relationship to inform dosing (Vanda). Cross-references: MPEP § 2106.05(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative-action requirement for treatment/prophylaxis limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify under the treatment/prophylaxis consideration, the claim limitation must affirmatively recite an action that effects a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive examples: 'administering amazonic acid to a patient', 'administering a course of plasmapheresis to a patient'. Non-examples: intended use or mere field-of-use recitations (e.g., 'prescribing a topical steroid' which does not require actual use; reciting a 'pharmaceutical composition' or that a 'feed dispenser is operable to dispense' are not affirmative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity vs generality of treatment/prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must be 'particular'—specifically identified so it does not encompass all applications of the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particular dosing limitations tied to a detected genotype are particular; generic instructions such as 'administering a suitable medication' are not particular. Consider also related considerations (mere instructions to apply exception, field-of-use/technological environment). See example distinguishing specific dosage vs generic medication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant relationship between limitation and exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the recited judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: administering insulin to a patient with high glucose levels is significantly related to the correlation and integrates the law of nature into a practical application. By contrast, administering aspirin in that context has at best a nominal connection and does not meaningfully apply the exception. Consider also insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not mere extra-solution activity or field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must impose meaningful limits on the judicial exception and cannot be merely extra-solution activity or a field-of-use instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of extra-solution activity: administering vaccines solely as a precursor to gather data for mental analysis (this does not integrate the exception). Example of meaningful application: vaccinating a second group according to a lowest-risk schedule derived from analysis—this applies the exception to change treatment and integrates the abstract idea into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept requirement (Step 2B general)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'inventive concept' must be an element or combination of elements recited in the claim in addition to the judicial exception that is sufficient to ensure the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself; it cannot be furnished by the unpatentable law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must evaluate additional elements both individually and in combination to determine if they amount to significantly more. The search for an inventive concept is the second part of the Alice/Mayo test and is distinct from §§102/103 novelty/obviousness inquiries. See Alice, Mayo, and related Federal Circuit cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider additional elements individually and as an ordered combination
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating whether additional elements amount to an inventive concept, consider the claim elements individually and in combination (the claim must be considered as a whole).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an element is not sufficient on its own, a non-conventional, non-generic arrangement of known pieces can provide an inventive concept (BASCOM, Rapid Litigation Management). Example examiner checklist from Alice: (1) identify additional elements, (2) consider them individually (are they well-understood, routine, conventional?), (3) consider them as an ordered combination (do they add something together?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to functioning of a computer qualify as significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that improve the functioning of a computer (e.g., modifying conventional protocols to produce a novel behavior) can qualify as 'significantly more'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: modification of Internet hyperlink protocol to dynamically produce a dual-source hybrid webpage (DDR Holdings). See MPEP § 2106.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to other technology or technical field qualify
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that improve a technology or technical field (outside computers) can qualify as significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: modifying rubber-molding processes to utilize a thermocouple inside the mold to reduce curing problems (Diehr). See MPEP § 2106.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying the judicial exception with/by a particular machine qualifies
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the judicial exception with or by use of a particular machine (with a specific structure arranged in a particular way) can supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: arranging a Fourdrinier machine components in a particular way to optimize speed while maintaining quality (Eibel Process). See MPEP § 2106.05(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article qualifies
rubrics_metrics.description: A process that effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing can be significantly more than a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: transforming raw, uncured synthetic rubber into precision-molded products (Diehr). See MPEP § 2106.05(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding specific, non-conventional limitations or unconventional steps qualifies
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a specific limitation other than well-understood, routine, conventional activity, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application, can amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: non-conventional arrangement of computer components for content filtering (BASCOM). See MPEP § 2106.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful limitations beyond linking to a technological environment qualify
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaningful limitations that do more than generally link the judicial exception to a particular technological environment may qualify as significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an immunization step integrating an abstract data-comparison idea into an actual immunizing process that lowers risk of later disease (Classen). See MPEP § 2106.05(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructions to 'apply it' or mere implementation on a computer are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding the words 'apply it' (or equivalent) or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer does not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: reciting that creating and maintaining electronic records is performed by a computer (Alice). See MPEP § 2106.05(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities at high generality is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level of generality to the judicial exception is not 'significantly more'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claims that require no more than a generic computer to perform generic computer functions. See Alice and related decisions; see MPEP § 2106.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering) to the judicial exception does not provide an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: obtaining information about transactions so it can be analyzed by an abstract mental process (CyberSource). See MPEP § 2106.05(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally linking the exception to a technological environment or field-of-use is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally linking use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use does not make the claim significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: limiting an abstract hedging idea to commodities markets or a mathematical formula to petrochemical fields (Bilski, Parker v. Flook). See MPEP § 2106.05(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicality/tangibility alone is not a relevant measure in Step 2B
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere physical or tangible implementation of an exception (e.g., 'a computer') is not by itself an inventive concept; conversely, lack of physicality does not doom a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of a computer or other tangible element is not decisive; courts have held that physical steps alone do not suffice (Alice, Genetic Technologies) and that non-physical improvements can be eligible when they improve a technological process (Enfish, McRO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for inventive concept is distinct from novelty/obviousness (§102/§103) and other §112 inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: The search for an inventive concept under §101 is separate from determinations of novelty (§102), non-obviousness (§103), and written description/enablement (§112); lack of novelty or obviousness is not dispositive of §101 and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute §102/§103/§112 analyses for the §101 inventive-concept inquiry. Prior art patentability is neither required for nor guarantees §101 eligibility. See Mayo, Diamond v. Diehr, Intellectual Ventures, Synopsys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-analysis checklist (how courts conduct Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts commonly: (1) identify additional elements in the claims; (2) consider those additional elements individually (are they well-understood, routine, conventional?); and (3) consider them as an ordered combination to determine whether together they add significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Alice's walk-through of identifying computer functions and hardware and concluding they were generic; BASCOM's instruction to consider arrangements in combination where a remote-filtering installation with customizable features provided an inventive concept. Use this as a practical examiner workflow.
